 Abstract 
 IV 
Abstract 
This bachelor thesis involves a structured literature review and a lightweight prototype in Python to 
analyse  Agentic  Artificial  Intelligence  (Agentic  AI)  for  the  purpose  of  task  automation.  It  examines 
the distinguishing features of Agentic AI over traditional chatbots and generative AI, details its core 
components like planning, memory/state, tool use, feedback and human oversight, and explores the 
potential   advantages   and   challenges,   such   as   reliability,   hallucination,   privacy,   security,   and 
accounta

potential   advantages   and   challenges,   such   as   reliability,   hallucination,   privacy,   security,   and

planning,  structured  data  interaction,  review,  bounded  revision,  human  approval  and  execution

Agentic AI has the potential to aid with multi-step task automation under controlled autonomy, limited

Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.1 Background and Context of the Study (Part 1)
chunks.content:
The  evolution  of  artificial  intelligence  (AI)  has  gone  from  a  rule- and  symbol-based  approach  to  a 
data-driven   machine   learning   paradigm,   and   more   recently,   a   large-scale   generative   model 
paradigm. Traditional AI involves a wide variety of methods to help machines execute tasks in the 
areas of perception, reasoning, problem solving, and decision making (Russell & Norvig, 2021). As 
more  and  more  data  and  computational  power  became  available,  machine-learning  and  deep-
learning approaches were developed where models learn patterns from the data rather than relying 
exclusively on manually-defined rules.  
An important technical step in this evolution was the transformer architecture, proposed by Vaswani 
et  al.  (2017).  Transformer  models  use  attention  operations  to  model  relationships  in  sequential 
information and are now the backbone of many trendy natural-language-processing programs. The 
development is taken one step further with large language models (LLMs), which are transformer-
based models trained on vast amounts of

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.1 Background and Context of the Study (Part 2)
chunks.content:
programs. The 
development is taken one step further with large language models (LLMs), which are transformer-
based models trained on vast amounts of textual data. For instance, Brown et al. (2020) showed that 
sufficiently scaled language models can be prompted to perform various tasks in natural language, 
without  updating  any  of  the  parameters  of  the  model,  and  that  they  can  learn  this  from  just  a  few 
examples.  These  advancements  helped  advance  the  use  of  generative  AI  systems  for  generating 
text,  summarising,  answering  questions,  programming  support,  and  other  knowledge-intensive 
tasks.  
However,  a  generative  language  model  does  not  necessarily  make  for  an  autonomous  or  agentic 
system. An LLM can be mainly used to generate outputs based on the context that it has been given, 
while  a  more  general  agent  design  can  also  include  planning,  maintained  state/memory,  external 
tools,  feedback,  and  action  execution/revision.  In  the  case  of  augmented  language  models,  these 
are systems that are extended beyon

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.1 Background and Context of the Study (Part 3)
chunks.content:
rnal 
tools,  feedback,  and  action  execution/revision.  In  the  case  of  augmented  language  models,  these 
are systems that are extended beyond the capabilities of language models with other functions and 
procedures,  such  as  reasoning.  Wang  et  al.  (2024)  also  spotlight  the  commonalities  among  LLM-
based autonomous-agent architectures: planning, memory, action, and interaction with the external 
environments. These advancements form the basis for the new Agentic AI conversation.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.2 Emergence of Agentic Artificial Intelligence
chunks.content:
Agentic  AI  can  be  thought  of  on  a  system  level  as  a  method  of  structuring  AI  parts  to  take  many 
sequential actions towards a given goal instead of simply providing a standalone answer. While the 
terminology is still evolving, modern studies on LLM-based agents have focused on systems that 1) 
understand a task goal, 2) break down the tasks into intermediate steps, 3) plan the agent's actions, 
4)  use  tools  and  information,  5)  track  relevant  state,  6)  reason  about  intermediate  results,  and  7) 
adapt subsequent steps (Wang et al., 2024). Agentic behaviour is not a specific feature of an LLM 
itself, but rather about structuring capabilities to execute a goal-oriented workflow. This distinction 
can  be  seen  in  the  approach  proposed  by  Yao  et  al.  (2023),  which  combines  reasoning  focused

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 1. Introduction (Part 1)
chunks.content:
2 
processing with actions for interaction with the external environment. These methods suggest ways 
in  which  language  models  can  be  integrated  with  other  models  to  support  a  cycle  of  decision, 
information and/or action seeking.  
This architecture applies to task automation as many practical tasks can't be done in one prompt-
response  interaction.  Intermediate  decisions  are  needed  to  create  a  study  schedule,  to  process 
information  from  a  number  of  sources,  to  organize  research  materials  or  to  coordinate  a  series  of 
administration activities, etc., and thus they deal with dependencies or constraints. At the same time, 
this  is  a  growing  complexity  in  the  workflow  which  leads  to  a  growing  need  for  system  control.  A 
system that produces a series of steps that are dependent on one another can carry an error from 
one step to another.  
Thus, thinking about Agentic AI as a way to increase autonomy is not enough. Responsible system 
design includes human supervision, validation mechanisms, restrictions on access to tools, and

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 1. Introduction (Part 2)
chunks.content:
to increase autonomy is not enough. Responsible system 
design includes human supervision, validation mechanisms, restrictions on access to tools, and the 
ability to interrupt and/or revise a workflow. Human centred AI research also explores the need for 
systems  to  maintain  important  human  control  and  to  enable  reliable  and  trustworthy  interaction 
(Shneiderman, 2020).

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.3 Research Problem (Part 1)
chunks.content:
The research question in this thesis stems from the dichotomy between the benefits of automated 
workflows  via  agents  and  the  potential  dangers  of  complex  AI-driven  decision-making  processes 
with  multiple  steps.  Typical  conversation  AI  systems  tend  to  generate  answers  to  individual  user 
input.  An  agentic  workflow,  on  the  other  hand,  can  create  and  implement  a  plan,  go  fetch  and/or 
process information from outside the system, take intermediate steps, evaluate the outcomes, and 
move on to a much larger goal. This broadened capacity can be utilized for more organized kinds of 
task mechanization, yet it likewise gives more chances to points of failure.  
This limitation of today's language-generation systems hallucination is still relevant. According to Ji 
et al. (2023), Hallucination refers to the creation of content that exceeds the content presented in the 
source or is not backed by the given information. This worry is not only as to the accuracy of one 
textual response, but also as to the correctness of the entire multi-step agentic wor

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.3 Research Problem (Part 2)
chunks.content:
n information. This worry is not only as to the accuracy of one 
textual response, but also as to the correctness of the entire multi-step agentic workflow. The goals 
may  impact  later  stages  as  a  result  of  incorrect  assumptions  in  goal  interpretation,  inappropriate 
planning decisions, incorrect calls of tools, or incorrect intermediate outputs. The privacy, security, 
reliability, evaluation, and accountability of agentic systems might also be concerns, as they can be 
interactive with the data and tools, unlike passive text generation (Wang et al., 2024).  
However,   much   research   has   already   been   conducted   in   the   academic   literature   regarding 
autonomous  agents,  augmented  language  models,  reasoning-and-action  patterns,  tool  use,  and 
LLM-based agent architectures. Hence, it can not be understood from this thesis that Agentic AI is 
an unexplored research area. What is missing, instead, is a synthesis of the key ideas, opportunities 
and challenges of Agentic AI for task automation at the bachelor level, in a structured way, and a

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.4 Aim and Objectives of the Thesis (Part 1)
chunks.content:
The objective of this thesis is to have a look at Agentic AI for task automation mainly from a literature-
based  perspective  and  to  showcase  some  characteristics  of  an  agentic  workflow  in  a  lightweight 
prototype  implemented  in  Python.  The  study  emphasizes  the  distinctions  between  Agentic  AI  and 
similar  types  of  AI,  the  key  components  of  an  AI  architecture  conducive  to  agentic  workflows,  the 
potential for task automation with AI agents, and the challenges and considerations of designing and 
implementing AI agents. 
To attain this objective, the thesis has six objectives: 
1. To create a solid conceptual understanding of Agentic AI and differentiate it from traditional 
chatbots,   general   generative   AI   systems,   robotic   process   automation,   and   previous 
autonomous-agent concepts.  
2. To  investigate  the  major  components  of  agentic  systems,  such  as  goal  interpretation, 
planning,  reasoning,  memory  or  state  maintenance,  use  of  tools,  feedback  and  human 
supervision.  
3. Analyse potential applications of Ag

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.4 Aim and Objectives of the Thesis (Part 2)
chunks.content:
planning,  reasoning,  memory  or  state  maintenance,  use  of  tools,  feedback  and  human 
supervision.  
3. Analyse potential applications of Agentic AI for task automation; productivity, personalisation, 
workflow support, educational planning.  
4. Evaluate and critically discuss the limitations of Agentic AI, such as hallucination, reliability, 
privacy, security, evaluation and accountability issues.  
5. To build a light weight Python prototype of a basic agentic study-task-planning workflow.  
6. To  make  practical  implications  for  responsible  design  and  controlled  use  of  Agentic  AI 
systems in computer science.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.5 Research Questions
chunks.content:
The research questions that guide the investigation are: 
RQ1: What is Agentic AI, and how does it differ from traditional chatbots and general generative AI 
systems? 
RQ2: What are the main components and workflow patterns of Agentic AI systems? 
RQ3: What opportunities does Agentic AI offer for task automation? 
RQ4: What challenges and limitations affect the safe and reliable use of Agentic AI? 
RQ5: How can a lightweight prototype demonstrate the basic workflow of an Agentic AI system?

chunks.content:
The thesis has mainly a literature based approach. Briefly summarises research on Agentic AI, LLM-
based agents, planning, tool interaction, feedback mechanisms and human oversight, opportunities 
for automation and the associated limitations. This practical is purposefully kept low level, a prototype 
in Python, for study-task planning. The prototype was developed to show the steps of converting a 
user goal into structured tasks, the use of local structured data, the comparison of structured tasks 
with structured criteria, and the human approval of structured tasks.  
This  reduced  implementation  is  in  line  with  the  implementation  scope  which  was  agreed  in  the 
approved exposé. There is no extensive experimentation, no humans in the study, no model training, 
or deployment. It does not measure real learning outcomes of the students and hence it does not 
assert  that  the  study  plans  produced  enhance  educational  achievement.  Likewise,  the  test  of 
usability of the prototype should not be used as a general indicator of the performance of Agentic AI.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 1.7 Academic and Practical Relevance
chunks.content:
The academic interest of the thesis is the opportunity to bring together literature from a number of 
related fields, and provide a coherent analysis of Agentic AI for task automation. These studies focus 
on various aspects of the larger issue, including augmented language models, autonomous agents, 
reasoning-and-action workflows, and hallucination (Ji et al., 2023; Mialon et al., 2023; Wang et al., 
2024; Yao et al., 2023).  
These  areas  can  be  brought  together  to  suggest  a  more  focused  analysis  of  the  how  goal 
interpretation,  planning,  tool  interaction,  feedback  and  supervision  can  contribute  to  an  agentic 
workflow. The usefulness is in showing how these concepts work in a real (albeit limited) software 
system. Instead of trying to construct a complicated agent system, the prototype is a clear system 
where  each  step  of  the  process  can  be  studied  independently.  This  allows  us  to  talk  about  what

This  thesis  used  the  structured  narrative  literature  review  as  the  main  research  design  which  has 
systematic  search  and  selection  components.  The  methodological  approach  is  suitable  since  the 
study aims to synthesise and critically analyse the existing knowledge of Agentic Artificial Intelligence 
(AAI) and not test a causal hypothesis in a controlled experiment. Well-executed, transparent and 
systematic literature reviews can be used as a research method in their own right, especially in areas 
of research that are rapidly changing and/or conceptually diverse (Snyder, 2019).  
The present study puts together a structured literature-search procedure and thematic synthesis for 
exploring the definitions of Agentic AI, its technical components, workflow patterns, opportunities for 
task   automation,   risks   and   implications   for   responsible   system   design.   The   literature-based 
investigation  is  backed  up  by  a  light-weight  Python  prototype.  The  prototype  does  not  aim  at  an 
experimental or production application of Agentic AI.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 2.2 Rationale for the Literature-Based Approach (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic   AI   combines   various   well-developed   and   new   fields   of   computer   science,   such   as 
autonomous  agents,  large  language  models,  tool-augmented  systems,  reasoning  and  planning, 
human AI interaction, and automation. As a result, knowledge on a topic is spread out across various 
journals,  conference  proceedings,  technical  surveys  and  institutional  publications.  The  use  of  a 
literature-based methodology allows these views to be explored in a comparative way, instead of on 
a single implementation or framework.  
When suitable, using proper procedures to collect and synthesize existing knowledge can serve to 
support theory development, conceptual clarification, and identifying research patterns as noted by 
Snyder  (2019).  This  is  especially  relevant  in  the  current  thesis  as  there  is  not  a  complete 
standardisation  of  terms  related  to  Agentic  AI.  The  structured  review  permits  a  comparison  of 
alternative  definitions  and  architectures,  without  assuming  that  one  framework  is  applicable  to  all

alternative  definitions  and  architectures,  without  assuming  that  one  framework  is  applicable  to  all

chunks.content:

The literature-search strategy has been designed in a way such that it is broad in scope, yet relevant. 
The  study  is  not  a  traditional  systematic  review  or  meta-analysis  but  a  search  with  a  structured 
narrative with explicit search, screening, and selection procedures. This is significant, as the thesis 
does  not  aim  to  provide  a  comprehensive  review  of  all  the  publications  on  AI  agents,  nor  does  it 
simply add up empirical results statistically.  
The  search  process  includes  both  database  search  using  keywords  and  selective  backward  and 
forward  reference  search  (exploration).  Reference  list  examination  can  find  influential  studies  that 
may not be the first to emerge in the keyword search and citation based forward searching may find 
later  work  that  builds  on  influential  studies.  According  to  Wohlin  (2014),  backward  and  forward 
snowballing  are  good  complementary  methods  for  getting  a  hold  on  what  literature  is  relevant, 
especially in software-engineering research.  
The  process  of  reporting

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 2.3 Literature Search Strategy (Part 2)
chunks.content:
tary  methods  for  getting  a  hold  on  what  literature  is  relevant, 
especially in software-engineering research.  
The  process  of  reporting  the  search  is  based  on  principles  of  transparency  of  structured-review 
guidance. The PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline for transparent reporting of systematic reviews is 
provided by Page et al. (2021). The present thesis does not however fully comply with PRISMA, as 
it  is  a  structured  narrative  review  not  a  formally  registered  systematic  review.  Therefore,  PRISMA 
rules  are  only  used  as  a  reference  point  to  transparent  document  identification,  screening and 
selection where these are applicable.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 2.7 Thematic Analysis
chunks.content:
The literature selected is then analysed thematically. Thematic analysis is a means of organising the 
data  into  patterns  and  themes  and  is  a  structured  way  of  identifying  the  patterns  from  complex

The  synthesis  follows  five  main  themes.  The  first  is  conceptual  and  has  to  do  with  the  difference 
between Agentic AI and other technologies. The second covers system architecture and workflow 
elements  such  as  planning,  memory,  use  of  tools,  feedback  and  human  supervision.  The  third 
focuses  on  possibilities  for  automation  of  tasks.  The  fourth  takes  into  account  risk,  limitation, 
governance  and  responsible  use.  The  fifth  relates  the  theoretical  findings  to  the  prototype  and  its 
design and interpretation. Sources can be used for more than one theme if applicable.

There  are  a  number  of  limitations  to  the  methodology.  The  structured  narrative  review  is  less

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.1 Development from Traditional AI to Agentic Systems (Part 1)
chunks.content:
11 
Artificial Intelligence refers to computational strategies that emulate perception, reasoning, learning, 
problem solving, decision making and other functions that normally would need the ability of a human 
being.  Previously,  AI  system  relied  heavily  on  symbolic  representations,  manually-specified  rules, 
search  procedures,  and  knowledge  bases.  For  such  systems  the  relationships  and  the  rules  for 
making decisions typically were hard-coded by the developers for a specific problem domain. While 
rule-based  methods  are  still  effective  whenever  the  processes  they  are  inferring  can  be  clearly 
stated,  they  are  not  as  effective  when  knowledge  of  what  is  relevant  is  not  fully  representable 
beforehand (Russell & Norvig, 2021). 
As  digital  data  and  computing  capabilities  became  more  readily  available,  approaches  based  on 
machine  learning – learning  from  examples  by  identifying  statistical  patterns – began  to  be  used. 
The next step was the advent of deep learning, which used multilayered neural networks that coul

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.1 Development from Traditional AI to Agentic Systems (Part 2)
chunks.content:
ifying  statistical  patterns – began  to  be  used. 
The next step was the advent of deep learning, which used multilayered neural networks that could 
learn  more  complicated  representations  from  larger  amounts  of  data.  Later,  the  transformer 
architecture became a key building block for more recent generative models in the field of natural 
language processing. Vaswani et al. (2017) proposed a transformer architecture which was mainly 
composed  of  attention  mechanisms,  which  allows  for  efficient  modelling  of  relationships  between 
elements in sequences, without relying on recurrent processing. 
The  upscalling  of  transformer-based  language  models  also  further  enhanced  the  capabilities  of 
generative AI. Brown et al. (2020) showed that a large autoregressive language model can be used 
to do a broad range of language tasks by simple zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting without 
task-specific  fine-tuning.  These  advances  have  led  to  more  general  conversation  and  generation 
systems. But creating a response to a stimulus is not the same

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.1 Development from Traditional AI to Agentic Systems (Part 3)
chunks.content:
tuning.  These  advances  have  led  to  more  general  conversation  and  generation 
systems. But creating a response to a stimulus is not the same as planning a series of moves to an 
overarching goal. 
Recent work on agents that leverage large-language models (LLMs) builds upon generative models 
and includes additional components such as planning, memory or maintained state, external tools, 
feedback, and interaction with an environment (Mialon et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Agentic AI 
can thus be seen as being a part of a larger trend of AI systems moving away from systems that only 
calculate or generate outputs to systems that coordinate multiple computation capabilities to achieve 
set goals. This evolution does not necessarily imply that the older approaches were "obsoleted" by 
the newer ones, in the sense of a chronological succession of methods. There is still a mix of rule-
based systems, machine learning, deep learning, generative models, and architectures that involve 
agents that may be combined, depending on the task.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.2 Machine Learning and Deep Learning Foundations (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Machine  learning  is  a  significant  paradigm  shift  from  rule-based programming, in which behaviour 
can  be  extracted  from  patterns  that  can  be  observed  in  the  data.  In  contrast,  supervised-learning 
systems  learn  mappings  from  examples,  in  which  the  examples  are  paired  with  labelled  outputs, 
while  unsupervised  learning  systems  find  structures  or  representations  in  the  absence  of  similar 
labelled outputs. Reinforcement learning is an additional paradigm where an agent learns through 
interacting and getting feedback from its environment (Russell & Norvig, 2021). Although they are 
very  different  from  current  Agentic  AI  they  offer  valuable  conceptual  underpinning  for  adaptive 
computational systems.  
Deep learning is an extension of machine learning that relies on neural architectures with a number 
of  representational  layers.  These  architectures  are  capable  of  learning  hierarchical  features  from 
complex  forms  of  data,  and  have  had  a  significant  impact, especially  in  computer  vision,  speech 
processing

chunks.content:
hierarchical  features  from 
complex  forms  of  data,  and  have  had  a  significant  impact, especially  in  computer  vision,  speech 
processing  and  natural  language  processing.  While  not  directly  relevant  to  Agentic  AI,  their 
significance is profound as contemporary language models are based on deep neural architectures 
and offer numerous language-processing and generation capabilities that can be further leveraged 
in Agentic AI systems.  
It is especially important in this context that the transformer has the architecture. Transformers do 
not take the tokens through a set of recurrent sequence operations, but instead self-attention is used 
to model relationships between elements of the input sequence (Vaswani et al., 2017). This design 
enables  parallel  processing  for  training  and  was  the  foundation  for  many  future  large  language 
models. However, neither deep learning nor the transformer architecture alone enables an agentic 
behaviour.  These technologies  enable  model  capabilities  which  can  be  composed  together  into 
multi-step workflo

chunks.content:
re alone enables an agentic 
behaviour.  These technologies  enable  model  capabilities  which  can  be  composed  together  into

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.3 Generative AI and Large Language Models (Part 1)
chunks.content:
13 
Generative  AI  is  a  broad  category  of  computational  systems  that  can  generate  new  content,  be  it 
text,  images,  code,  or  something  else,  from  learned  distributions.  The  most  relevant  form  in  the 
context  of  this  thesis  is  language  generation  the  LLM.  These  models  can  be  trained  with  vast 
amounts  of  text  data  and  produce  relevant  continuation  of  text,  follow  instructions,  summarize, 
answer questions and many other aspects of knowledge work.  
Brown et al. (2020) illustrated the importance of scaling for prompt-based task performance: if the 
language model is sufficiently large, it can learn the various tasks from the examples. But this type 
of  flexibility  shouldn't  be  confused  with  system  autonomy.  LLM  usually  outputs  based  on  an  input 
context; it doesn't have a persistent goal, it can't access external tools, and it doesn't have its own 
workflow execution mechanism.  
The difference between the two is at the heart of Agentic AI. According to Mialon et al. (2023), LLM 
capabilities are expanded by augmentin

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.3 Generative AI and Large Language Models (Part 2)
chunks.content:
hanism.  
The difference between the two is at the heart of Agentic AI. According to Mialon et al. (2023), LLM 
capabilities are expanded by augmenting language models with reasoning procedures, retrieval and 
tools. The use of tools is especially significant as it enables a language model to leverage resources 
outside of itself. For instance, Schick et al. (2023) showed that language models can be trained to 
know when and how to use external tools like calculators, search mechanisms and other APIs with 
a model called Toolformer. This kind of study exemplifies the shift from language model to be used 
as a generator of text to language model as a part of a larger computational process.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.4 Defining Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Part 1)
chunks.content:
As of now, there is no one common definition of Agentic AI. There is overlap in the terminology with 
research  into  intelligent  agents,  autonomous  agents,  LLM-based  agents,  augmented  language 
models, and multi-agent systems. As such, it is better to define it from a system level point of view 
rather than to think of Agentic AI as a separate technical category.  
Agentic  AI  is  an  AI  powered  system  architecture  that  performs  a  desired  task  via  a  series  of 
coordinated  operations  that  include  the  specification  of  the  task  and  goal,  planning,  maintaining 
appropriate  state,  interacting  with  tools  or  data,  assessing  intermediate  results,  adapting  actions, 
etc., with a given degree of human oversight. This definition does not imply that all agents have to 
include  all  these  components,  but  rather  common  architectural  components  found  in  the  current 
LLM-agent literature (Mialon et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024).  
Based on elements like profiling, memory, planning, action, etc., Wang et al. (2024) categorise LLM-
based  autonomo

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.4 Defining Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Part 2)
chunks.content:
al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024).  
Based on elements like profiling, memory, planning, action, etc., Wang et al. (2024) categorise LLM-
based  autonomous-agent  architectures.  Their  analysis  shows  that  the  language  model  itself  is 
crucial part in the reasoning and interaction process but it is working inside an agent architecture. 
Yao  et  al.  (2023)  convey  this  system  level  difference  in  a  similar  manner,  with  ReAct,  which  pairs 
reasoning-related processing with actions that affect an external environment.  
Therefore, an LLM need not necessarily be called an ‘agent’. A conversational model which responds 
to  a  single  question  can  exhibit  complex  language  skills  without  holding  or  controlling  a  goal  or  a

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 3. Conceptual Foundations of Agentic Artificial Intelligence
chunks.content:
14 
series  of  actions.  Agentic  properties  are  manifested  in  the  organisation  of  models,  tools,  state-
management mechanisms and control processes, oriented towards achieving a task.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.5 Characteristics and Degrees of Autonomy (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic systems are generally described in terms of the following capabilities, which are also very 
common. Goal orientation is a source of a goal around which actions are organised. Planning and 
task  decomposition  are  related  to  breaking  down  large  objectives  into  smaller,  intermediate  ones. 
Memory  or  maintained  state:  relevant  information  from  previous  stages  to  affect  subsequent 
operations.  Tool  interaction:  can  tell  the  system  to  get  information  or  perform  actions  beyond  the 
language model itself. Feedback and revision allow for the evaluation and also reversion of outputs 
prior to finalisation (Mialon et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024).  
Such capabilities are not an indication of unlimited autonomy. Autonomy should be considered as a 
spectrum  of  what  decisions  and  actions  are  allowed  to  be  made  by  the  system  without  the  direct 
influence of humans. On the one hand, an AI system can only recommend a plan that needs to be 
accepted  by  a  human.  On  another  level,  it  can  perform  specific  tools  that  are  low  risk

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.5 Characteristics and Degrees of Autonomy (Part 2)
chunks.content:
stem can only recommend a plan that needs to be 
accepted  by  a  human.  On  another  level,  it  can  perform  specific  tools  that  are  low  risk  without  a 
confirmation, and specific tools that are consequential require confirmation. Several steps may be 
coordinated independently by more autonomous architectures within pre-specified boundaries.  
Thus human supervision is important conceptually. Bounded autonomy is about an agentic system 
having  the  ability  to  run  beneficial  multi-step  processes  with  restrictions  like  approved  tool  sets, 
iteration  limits,  validation  requirements,  etc.,  and  human  approval.  Such  limits  do  not  negate  the 
ability  of  a  system  to  show  agentic  characteristics;  rather  they  are  a  definition  of  the  range  of  the 
characteristics  that  may  be  shown.  Likewise,  the  memory  should  not  be  understood  as  being 
universal,  or  permanently present.  Some  of  the  implementations  store  only  short  term  execution 
state;  others  utilize  persistent  stores  in  order  to  retrieve  information  over

chunks.content:
f  the  implementations  store  only  short  term  execution 
state;  others  utilize  persistent  stores  in  order  to  retrieve  information  over  longer  time  periods.  The 
choice of design will be dictated by the application requirements, privacy considerations, reliability 
requirements, and the length of time the task is to be performed.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.6 Comparison with Traditional Chatbots and Generative AI Assistants
chunks.content:
Traditional chatbots are mainly reactive, meaning that they are systems that react to user messages. 
Previous implementations have been based on such as predefined rules, decision trees, intents or 
retrieval mechanisms. Thus, their behaviour was limited to the conversational logic in the application. 
These systems can be effective at automating customer interactions but conventionally do not devise 
and execute flexible multi-step plans.  
Modern  generative  AI  assistants  offer  significantly  more  linguistic  flexibility  as  they  are  able  to 
understand  natural  language  instructions  and  create  original  responses.  They  might  condense  a 
text,  compose  a  program,  explain  ideas,  or  make  suggestions.  However,  a  generative  assistant 
working  in  a  traditional  prompt-response  style  does  not  automatically  mean  that  it's  agentic.  The 
main difference is about the way workflow is orchestrated, not the quality of the generated output.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 3. Conceptual Foundations of Agentic Artificial Intelligence
chunks.content:
15 
An agentic system can make use of a generative model to interpret a goal and then to select what 
intermediate  operations  are  to  be  performed,  what  tools  are  available  (that  are  permitted  for  the 
agent to use), maintain a state of the agent's tasks, evaluate the results, and decide whether or not 
to  perform  more  operations.  The  separation  between  generative  assistants  and  Agentic  AI  can 
therefore  be  not  well-defined.  Today's  assistants  can  even  start  to  use  tools,  use  memory,  and 
execute  multiple  steps,  making  them  show  agent-like  capabilities.  These  categories,  therefore, 
should  be  viewed  as  architectural  patterns  that  overlap  and  are  not  mutually  exclusive  product 
categories.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.7 Comparison with Robotic Process Automation and Earlier Autonomous Agents (Part 1)
chunks.content:
One other significant comparison is robotic process automation (RPA). RPA is typically employed to 
automate structured and repetitive business processes with software robots that communicate with 
existing software applications. According to van der Aalst et al. (2018), RPA is a way of automating 
repetitive information systems interactions and Syed et al. (2020) describe common RPA tasks as 
being relatively rule-based, structured and repetitive.  
Agentic AI stands out primarily for its ability to understand less structured goals and to perform goal-
dependent  action  selection.  For  instance,  while  traditional  RPA  typically  adheres  strictly  to  a  set 
sequence of actions, an LLM-based agent could dynamically create or adjust a plan based on the 
situation. This flexibility also adds a dose of uncertainty: deterministic automation is more apt for a 
precisely specified and predictable work flow, while an agentic architecture is more appropriate when 
interpretation, planning and adaptation are needed.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.8 Conceptual Synthesis
chunks.content:
The  comparison  illustrates  that  Agentic  AI  doesn't  necessarily  represent  a  new  type  of  language 
model but rather an architectural pattern at the system level. The focus of traditional chatbots is on 
"reactive" communication, while RPA is focused on automating processes with pre-defined actions, 
and generative assistants are focused on generating creative and flexible content. Agentic systems 
take a hybrid of these approaches but add an increased focus on the interpretation of goals, planning, 
state   management,   interaction   with   tools,   feedback,   and   coordinated   multi-step   action.   The

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 3. Conceptual Foundations of Agentic Artificial Intelligence
chunks.content:
17 
difference between the two is however only relative. As increasingly more capabilities are introduced 
to  a  generative  assistant,  such  as  planning,  access  to  tools,  memory  and  workflow  control,  the 
assistant   can   become   more   agentic.   An   agent   can   also   have   components   for   deterministic 
automation of specific actions, similarly. Thus, the question to be explored with regard to any system 
is  not  just  whether  it  is  an  “agent”,  but  what  kinds  of  agency,  autonomy,  control  and  external 
interaction the architecture allows.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.9 Chapter Summary (Part 1)
chunks.content:
In this chapter, the difference between Agentic AI and traditional chatbots and general generative AI 
systems was explored by examining the definition of Agentic AI. The analysis suggests that Agentic 
AI can be viewed as a system architecture that generally structures the AI models around a multi-
step  activity  with  a  well-defined  goal  in  mind.  An  agentic  system  might  consist  of  a  mix  of  goal 
interpretation,  planning,  maintained  state,  external  tool  interaction,  feedback,  revision,  and  action 
control, which are not typical of a chatbot or one-shot generative model. An LLM can thus be a crucial 
part  of  an  agentic  architecture  but  not  an  agent  in  and  of  itself.  Agentic  AI  also  stands  out  from 
traditional  RPA,  which  usually  automates  more  structured  and  predefined  tasks,  allowing  agentic 
systems to potentially adjust intermediate steps for less structured goals. Agentic AI, however, is not 
a replacement for the previous intelligent agent concepts but an evolution of the same. Its current 
relevance  is  mainly  due  to  its

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 3.9 Chapter Summary (Part 2)
chunks.content:
ever, is not 
a replacement for the previous intelligent agent concepts but an evolution of the same. Its current 
relevance  is  mainly  due  to  its  integration  of  traditional  notions  of  computational  agency  with  the 
adaptability  of  language,  reasoning,  and  tool  interactions  of  modern  LLMs.  Chapter  4  discusses 
these architectural elements and their interactions in more detail.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.2 Goal Interpretation and Task Decomposition (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Goal interpretation is used to define the task of an agentic system. Natural language requests can 
include   implicit   requirements   and   ambiguous   terms,   deadlines,   limitations   on   resources,   or 
conflicting  constraints.  An  agent  thus  needs  some  way  to  translate the  initial  instruction  into  a 
representation that can be executed and which will be used to determine subsequent steps. It could 
be a structured object, an explicit list of requirements or the state that is carried around as context 
throughout the workflow, based on the architecture.  
Task decomposition is a step after the goal interpretation, in which a goal is broken down into smaller 
operations.  This  particularly  useful  when  a  goal  can't  be  reliably  achieved  in  one  generation  step. 
One of the common components of LLM-agent architectures is planning, which is seen in Wang et 
al. (2024), and reasoning-related processing can be interleaved with the actions in the environment 
as shown in Yao et al. (2023).  
While decomposition can simplify a workflow, it also introduces depe

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.2 Goal Interpretation and Task Decomposition (Part 2)
chunks.content:
interleaved with the actions in the environment 
as shown in Yao et al. (2023).  
While decomposition can simplify a workflow, it also introduces dependencies; if the interpretation is 
wrong throughout, then all the following tasks will be affected. Decomposition should be limited by 
the information that is explicitly available and the capabilities of the system for this reason. Coherent-
looking but infeasible plan can be generated by an agent that does not consider the availability of 
tools  and/or  does  not  observe  temporal,  financial  and  safety  constraints.  The  validation  of  goal 
interpretation  and  decomposition  are  thus  desirable  prior  to  their  execution,  especially  in  systems 
with external capabilities.  
The  general  process  shown  in  Fig  3  allows  planning,  action,  review  and  revision  to  be  interlinked 
and not distinct steps.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.3 Planning and Reasoning (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Planning is important to move an agent from a well-defined goal to a sequence of actions. Planning 
can  be  as  simple  as  creating  a  sequence  of  tasks  in  relatively  simple  systems.  More  complicated 
architectures can adapt the plan based upon new observations, for example. There is no "one best 
way to plan" described in the literature, but planning varies depending on task structure, capability 
of the model, uncertainty in the environment and the level of autonomy allowed.  
ReAct offers a powerful model for the interaction of reasoning-related processing with action. Instead 
of  the  language  generation  and  interaction  with  the  environment  being  two  distinct  phases,  this 
approach involves an intertwined process between the internal language generation task and actions 
that give rise to new observations from the environment (Yao et al., 2023). It's about the approach 
and having Agentic AI think for itself to work, rather than simply being given a fixed starting point in 
the form of a prompt.  
In this thesis, reasoning is seen as a functional one: it is

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.3 Planning and Reasoning (Part 2)
chunks.content:
o work, rather than simply being given a fixed starting point in 
the form of a prompt.  
In this thesis, reasoning is seen as a functional one: it is reasoning that is performed on a computer 
to select, order, or evaluate actions. It should not be regarded as proof of 'cognition' in the sense of 
human  cognition.  Moreover,  there  is  no  need  to  reproduce  all  the  models'  chain  of  thought  in  an 
unrestricted manner; it is not desirable to do so when documenting an agentic architecture. Selected 
actions,  structured  plans,  validation  results  and  execution  traces  are  more  directly  applicable  to 
system design transparency and reproducibility.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.4 Memory and Context Management (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic  workflows  often  need  to  use  data  from  previous  actions  to  determine  future  actions.  This 
continuity  is  provided  by  Memory  or  maintained  state.  On  the  other  hand,  Wang  et  al.  (2024) 
differentiate between memory as a key design feature of LLM-based agents, and Park et al. (2023) 
present a more sophisticated design in which experiences are stored and retrieved, and combined 
to aid reflection and planning in generative agents. Memory can be at various levels. Short term state 
can  include  the  current  task,  previous  completed  tasks,  results  of  tools  and  active  constraints. 
Persistence  over  sessions,  or  longer-term  memory,  is  not  necessary  for  agentic  behaviour,  but  is 
possible in longer-term memory. Architectures should thus not rely on the fact that more memory is 
better.  
In context management you have to make compromises. An insufficient amount of information may 
result in the agent discarding useful constraints or reprovisioning itself with redundant information. 
Often if too much or irrelevant information is ret

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.4 Memory and Context Management (Part 2)
chunks.content:
lt in the agent discarding useful constraints or reprovisioning itself with redundant information. 
Often if too much or irrelevant information is retrieved, the quality of the decision may be reduced, 
or  the  cost  of  computation  may  be  increased.  Persistent  memory  also  poses  privacy  and  data-
retention  issues.  Memory  should  therefore  be  designed  with  the  minimal  state  that  the  planned 
workflow needs for its operation in mind and not as a free repository of the interaction history.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.5 Tool Use and External Data Interaction (Part 1)
chunks.content:
22 
Unlike many conventional prompt-response systems, the use of tools can enable the system to get 
information, to make calculations, to access files, to interact with software or to take any other action 
allowed.  One  approach  to  extending  language  models  past  their  parameterized  knowledge  is  to 
augment  them  with  tools,  as  done  by  Mialon  et  al.  (2023).  Toolformer  exemplifies  a  model-based 
approach to using tools.  
Schick et al. (2023) explore strategies for controlling when to use and what to use external tools for, 
and  how  to  integrate  their  results  into  the  later  generations.  The  takeaway  from  this  is  that  not  all 
agents  need  to  use  Toolformer,  but  that  with  the  integration  of  external  computation  in  language-
model   workflows,   the   model   doesn't   have   to   generate   all   information   on   its   own.   From   an 
architectural point of view, it's desirable that the tool interface separate the agent's requests from the 
actual tool use. This allows for tool use validation, restriction of permissions, tracki

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.5 Tool Use and External Data Interaction (Part 2)
chunks.content:
at the tool interface separate the agent's requests from the 
actual tool use. This allows for tool use validation, restriction of permissions, tracking of tool use, and 
denial of unsupported actions. An agent's capabilities can thus be extended by providing it with tools, 
but also its risk surface. The implications to a system are very different if it can read a local structured 
file vs one that has unrestricted external permissions. The right architecture is important based on 
the implications of failure.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.6 Feedback, Reflection, and Revision (Part 1)
chunks.content:
First  model  outputs  may  not  be  good  enough,  hence  architectures  with  feedback  and  iterative 
refinement. Self-Refine is an iterative process where an initial output is generated by an LLM and 
then it provides feedback on that output and tries to generate an improved one (Madaan et al., 2023). 
This method shows a refinement pattern, and doesn't require any additional trained reward model.  
Reflexion  is  more  directed  towards  learning  from  feedback  in  subsequent  attempts.  Shinn  et  al. 
(2023) suggest that linguistic reflections, based on task feedback, be stored in an episodic memory 
buffer  and  be  used  for  subsequent  attempts.  This  is  not  the  standard  parameter-based  RL  as  the 
model weights do not undergo changes in the reflection process.  
The ideas should not be taken as proof that self-evaluation can be relied upon all the time. A model 
that  outputs  wrong  model  output  can  be  used  to  infer  wrong/inaccurate  model  output.  Therefore, 
there may be a benefit of a reviewing/criticism system, but it does not eliminate the need for

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.6 Feedback, Reflection, and Revision (Part 2)
chunks.content:
o  infer  wrong/inaccurate  model  output.  Therefore, 
there may be a benefit of a reviewing/criticism system, but it does not eliminate the need for external 
validation  where  there  are  errors  to  be  made.  Unrestricted  iterative  refinement  is  particularly 
significant  in  that  it  has  the  potential  to  add  to  the  cost  of  the  calculation  while  not  ensuring 
convergence. In real-world agentic systems, there are iteration limits, explicit validation criteria and 
escalation to human review, which give some clear bounds to the operation of the system.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.7 Single-Agent and Multi-Agent Workflow Patterns
chunks.content:
Agentic workflows can be structured with one agent or many agents that are interacting with each 
other.  In  a  single  agent  system  the  goal  interpretation,  planning,  selecting  the  appropriate  tools, 
action  and  review  are  all  carried  out  by  a  single  component.  This  may  decrease  the  amount  of

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 4. Architecture and Workflow of Agentic AI Systems (Part 1)
chunks.content:
23 
communication, and simplify the management of the state. Hence it can be used for many bounded 
workflows which don't benefit a lot from role separation.  
In the multi-agent architectures, several agents or conversational roles are responsible for different 
tasks. For instance, AutoGen supports multiple LLM-powered agents that engage in conversations 
and collaborate on various tasks within an application (Wu et al., 2024). This work was first presented 
as  a  preprint  and  at  various  workshops  prior  to  its  publication  in  2024  in  the  First  Conference  on 
Language  Modeling.  These  architectures  can  be  based  on  the  separation  of  planning,  execution, 
critique  or  domain-specific  responsibilities,  but  make  more  agents  doesn't  mean  better.  They  also 
add  communication  overhead,  coordination  needs  and  additional  possibilities  for  propagation  of 
errors between agents.  
Generative  Agents  are  another  architecture  that  shows  how  multiple  agents  can  be  used  to  show 
multi-component  agent  behaviour,  not  just  multiple  spe

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 4. Architecture and Workflow of Agentic AI Systems (Part 2)
chunks.content:
are  another  architecture  that  shows  how  multiple  agents  can  be  used  to  show 
multi-component  agent  behaviour,  not  just  multiple  specialised  agents.  Park  et  al.  (2023)  fuse 
observation,   memory   retrieval,   reflection   and   planning   to   simulate interactive   agents.   The 
contribution shows that agentic behaviour can be based on an organization of memory and planning 
over time, and not only on language generation. Therefore, the single agent or multi-agent systems 
should   be   determined   by   functional   requirements.   Role   separation,   specialised   context   and 
collaboration are all good reasons for using a multi-agent architecture, but in other cases, additional 
complexity might impede interpretability and make things more expensive.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.8 Human-in-the-Loop Supervision and Bounded Autonomy (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic AI doesn't necessarily need to be fully automated. Human-in-the-loop design rather views 
human control as an integral part of the system design. Design guidelines for human–AI interaction 
are  offered  by  Amershi  et  al.  (2019),  and  this  stresses  the importance  of  proper  communication, 
control  and  correction  as  well  as  feedback.  Shneiderman  (2020)  also  contends  that  the  level  of 
automation can coexist with meaningful human control, and should not be seen as design objectives 
that  conflict.  He  uses  his human-centred  AI  approach  to  focus  on  robust,  safe  and  trustworthy  AI 
systems with human responsibility.  
In  agentic  workflows,  bounded  autonomy  can  be  achieved  by  restricting  access  to  tools,  setting  a 
max number of iterations, adding approval points, enforcing validation rules, maintaining execution 
logs and providing for cancellation. There must be an appropriate level of supervision based upon 
risk.  A  consequence  profile  differs  from  the  automatic  formatting  of  a  local  study  schedule,  with 
external

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.8 Human-in-the-Loop Supervision and Bounded Autonomy (Part 2)
chunks.content:
of supervision based upon 
risk.  A  consequence  profile  differs  from  the  automatic  formatting  of  a  local  study  schedule,  with 
external communications or the changing of financial data. As systems become more agentic, there 
are  governance  and  accountability  issues,  argue  Shavit  et  al.  (2023),  as  they  may  have  complex 
objectives and not be directly supervised. They focus on practices within their governance structure 
that are designed to ensure agent operations are safer and more accountable, but also recognise 
outstanding implementation issues. It is not an empirical, peer-reviewed paper, but is a White Paper 
written  by  institutions  and  should  be  interpreted  as  guidance  in  governance,  not  necessarily  as 
experimental evidence.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.9 ReAct and Related Agentic Patterns (Part 1)
chunks.content:
The  research  directions  presented  here  in  this  chapter  tackles  distinct  architectural  issues  and 
should not be regarded as alternative agent architectures. The area of ReAct is to connect reasoning 
related processing with action in the environment (Yao et al., 2023). Toolformer is an exploration of 
when  and  how  language  models  can  benefit  from  external  tools  (Schick  et  al.,  2023).  Self-Refine 
adds iterative feedback and refinement within generation (Madaan et al., 2023), while Reflexion adds 
verbal feedback to episodic memory which can impact subsequent attempts (Shinn et al., 2023). AI 
Chains aims to increase the control and transparency of complex tasks involving LLM, by using chain 
of prompting (Wu et al., 2022).  
Persistent  simulated  agents  (Park  et  al.,  2023)  are  simulated  agents  that  focus  on  memory, 
reflection,  and  planning.  AutoGen  emphasizes  talk  orchestration  multi-agents  (Wu  et  al.,  2024). 
Instead,  AgentBench  is  defined  as  more  an  evaluation  framework  than  an  architecture.  Liu  et  al. 
(2024) analyze

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.9 ReAct and Related Agentic Patterns (Part 2)
chunks.content:
(Wu  et  al.,  2024). 
Instead,  AgentBench  is  defined  as  more  an  evaluation  framework  than  an  architecture.  Liu  et  al. 
(2024) analyze the performance of LLMs as agents in interactive settings, emphasising the need to 
measure agent capabilities based on their behaviour over a series of actions, not just on the quality 
of text generation. AgentBench was unveiled at ICLR 2024.  
As  a  whole,  these  works  indicate  that  there  is  no  convergence  of  the  workflow  for  contemporary 
Agentic AI research. Rather, it considers alternative approaches to planning, using tools, memory, 
iterative  refinement,  multi-agent  coordination  and  evaluation. The  correct  mix  should  be  identified 
based   upon   the   task   requirements   and   not   necessarily   maximizing   the   number   of   Agentic 
components.

chunks.content:

This  chapter  answered  the  RQ2:  What  are  the  key  elements  and  the  processes  of  Agentic  AI 
systems?  As  per  the  literature,  the  goal  interpretation,  task  decomposition,  planning,  maintained 
state/memory,  tool  interaction,  action  generation,  review,  feedback, revision,  execution  monitoring 
and  human  oversight  are  some  of  the  common  components  of  an  agentic  architecture.  These 
functions can be realised either in a single orchestrating agent or in different parts, or in specialised 
agents.  
The analysis also reveals that there is no single architecture that can be used to represent Agentic 
AI.   ReAct,   Toolformer,   Self-Refine,   Reflexion,   AI   Chains,   Generative   Agents,   AutoGen   and 
AgentBench  focus  on  various  aspects  of  agentic  behaviour  and  assessment.  Planning  and  tool 
interaction  go  beyond  just  isolated  generation,  memory  adds  continuity,  feedback  and  revision 
enable iteration and improvement, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms put operational boundaries 
around automation.  
So,  the  answe

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 4.10 Chapter Summary (Part 2)
chunks.content:
ck  and  revision 
enable iteration and improvement, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms put operational boundaries 
around automation.  
So,  the  answer  to  RQ2  is  that  Agentic  AI  systems  generally  exhibit  the  following  properties: 
Coherent,  Goal-driven  Process  Execution:  They  involve  coordinated  process  execution  with  a 
selected set of mechanisms for planning, managing state, interacting with the external environment, 
receiving feedback, and controlling execution. The mechanisms needed will vary depending on the 
level  of  complexity  and  risk  of  the  task,  the  tools  available,  the  level  of  reliability  required,  and 
acceptable  level  of  autonomy. This  architectural  view  will  form  the  foundation  of  Chapter  5  where 
these capabilities are explored in the context of practical applications in the field of task automation.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.1 Agentic AI as an Approach to Task Automation (Part 1)
chunks.content:
26 
Task automation has been a longtime staple of activities that can be codified in rules, workflows or 
software connections. For instance, robotic process automation (RPA) is well-suited for structured 
and repetitive processes where the order of tasks to be performed is quite predictable (van der Aalst 
et al., 2018). Agentic AI takes the automation conversation one step further into tasks where more 
interpretation,   decomposition,   contextual   adaptation,   and/or   interaction   with   a   diverse   set   of 
information sources are needed. An agentic system can be used to try to interpret an objective and 
break  down  the  intermediate  tasks,  utilize  allowed  tools,  assess  results  and  modify  subsequent 
action.  
The promise is therefore not so much in the ability to replace existing automation technology, but in 
that of tackling tasks which are hard to formulate a priori. According to Wang et al. (2024), some of 
the most commonly recurring dimensions of LLMs-based autonomous agents are planning, memory, 
action and interaction. In a similar fashion, Mialon et a

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.1 Agentic AI as an Approach to Task Automation (Part 2)
chunks.content:
he most commonly recurring dimensions of LLMs-based autonomous agents are planning, memory, 
action and interaction. In a similar fashion, Mialon et al. (2023) define augmented language models 
as language-models that are able to use tools and provide reasoning abilities. If these functions can 
be  integrated into  a  structured  process,  an  AI  system  can  assist  with  tasks  that  involve  multiple 
sequential steps or stages, and not just a single generation.  
This  capability  does  not  necessarily  equate  to  an  organisational  benefit  however  and  should  be 
distinguished from such. Just because an agentic workflow process is technically possible, doesn't 
necessarily mean that this will boost productivity, accuracy or quality. This is still dependent on task 
characteristics, reliability of underlying model, information that is available, design of the tools and 
human supervision.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.2 Productivity and Workflow Efficiency (Part 1)
chunks.content:
A  possible  use  case  for  Agentic  AI  is  to  decrease  the  amount  of  manual  coordination  needed  for 
multi-step  knowledge  work.  While  conventional  generative  AI  might  generate  a  specific  answer, 
summary,  or  recommendation,  an  agentic  workflow  has  the  potential  to  break  down  a  bigger 
objective  into  smaller  tasks  and  orchestrate  them  one  by  one.  An  example  is  the  model-based 
processing in ReAct, which allows for environmental action, with information gained during the model 
processing being used to inform subsequent actions.  
This design can provide productivity for users who otherwise would have to manually switch back 
and  forth  between  applications,  information  sources,  and  in-between  decisions.  This  can  be 
arranging a series of tasks, gathering data from those who have been approved, or even seeing if 
specific requirements have been met in a defined plan. But in such cases, it might be most efficient 
to minimize the coordination overhead, not the need for humans.  
But the more progress made toward automation, the

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.2 Productivity and Workflow Efficiency (Part 2)
chunks.content:
ases, it might be most efficient 
to minimize the coordination overhead, not the need for humans.  
But the more progress made toward automation, the more can go wrong. A plan may not be suitable 
even if it was "generated" by a tool, or a tool may present only partial information, or an intermediate

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 5. Opportunities of Agentic AI for Task Automation
chunks.content:
27 
error  may  lead  to  further  errors.  Agentic  automation  is  most  beneficial  when  the  workflow  can  be 
tracked,  and  that  the  intermediate  products  can  be  reviewed.  Research  on  human–AI  interaction 
highlights the need to communicate, correct, and take charge of processes aided by an AI system 
and not to automate everything for the betterment of the user (Amershi et al., 2019; Shneiderman, 
2020).

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.3 Personalised and Context-Aware Assistance (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic  architectures  can  further  facilitate  more  context-aware  assistance  because  they  can  keep 
information  about  the  task  at  hand,  and  reuse  it  throughout  multiple  parts  of  the  workflow.  Unlike 
one-off   prompt-response   exchange,   maintained   state   enables   an   application   to   take   into 
consideration objectives it has recognized before, activities it has finished, user restrictions, or the 
results  of  the  tool.  Wang  et  al.  (2024)  propose  memory  to  be  an  essential  architectural  aspect  of 
LLM-based agents, and Park et al. (2023) show that observations and retrieved information could 
be useful for planning and behaviour in generative-agent simulations.  
For  individual  productivity,  they  might  be  useful  for  programs  scheduling  goals  and  priorities, 
rearranging schedules when constraints change, or keeping things going during an extended activity. 
However, care must be taken with the scope of personalisation. However, there can be privacy or 
data-retention   issues   with   persistent   memory;   if   the   memo

chunks.content:
be taken with the scope of personalisation. However, there can be privacy or 
data-retention   issues   with   persistent   memory;   if   the   memory   improperly   indicates   a   user's 
preferences, then inappropriate recommendations are produced. Good context-aware support thus 
needs  more  than  just  more  information – it  requires  the  selection  of  relevant  information  and 
maintenance of user control.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.4 Educational Support and Study Planning (Part 1)
chunks.content:
An application context that is relevant is that of education, where a large number of activities related 
to   studying   can   be   highly   beneficial   from   a   planning,   prioritisation,   scheduling,   information 
organisation  and  progress  monitoring  perspective.  Zawacki-Richter  et  al.  (2019)  conducted  a 
systematic  review  of  the  use  of  AI  in  higher  education,  and  found  a  wide  array  of  AI-assisted 
educational activities. It is important to understand that their review is before the current creation of 
LLM-based  Agentic  AI systems  and  can't  be  considered  as  a  direct  example  of  today's  agentic 
systems. However, it states that educational planning, support and assessment and personalisation 
has long been recognized to be areas of relevant AI applications.  
An  agentic  study-support  system  could  be  given  a  broad  task,  such  as  preparation  towards  an 
examination in a given time frame, and break it down into smaller tasks. Study time may be regarded 
as a constraint, subjects may be given priorities and a draft schedule may

chunks.content:
e frame, and break it down into smaller tasks. Study time may be regarded 
as a constraint, subjects may be given priorities and a draft schedule may be checked for workload 
or deadline conflicts. The plan may be adjusted if something changed the goal would stay the same. 
This use case is related to the prototype shown in Chapter 7. The prototype is intended to illustrate 
architectural   concepts   such   as   goal   interpretation,   structured   data   access,   planning,   review, 
bounded  revision,  and  human  approval. Its  implementation  does  not  demonstrate  that  Agentic  AI

to be designed, which is not possible in the scope of this thesis.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.5 Business and Administrative Workflow Support (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Business  and  administrative  processes  have  both  structured  and  less  structured  processes.  RPA 
has proven to be applicable for automating repetitive interactions with existing information systems, 
especially in situations where the inputs, process rules, and outputs are relatively stable (Syed et al., 
2020; van der Aalst et al., 2018). Processes that can be defined as fixed rules can be automated by 
agentic AI but sometimes need interpretation or adaptation, which can be done by agentic AI.  
These can be, among other things, sorting incoming information, creating initial to-do lists, gathering 
data  from  authorised  sources,  assisting  processes  of  document  processing,  or  marking  tasks  that 
need to be done by humans. AI architectures can also be multi-step, with various functional roles, 
like  planning,  execution,  and  review.  But,  for  more  deterministic  and  more  volume  processes, 
conventional  RPA  might  be  better  as  predictable  rule-based  execution  can  be  simpler  to  validate 
and audit. Thus, agentic AI shouldn't be considered a “one

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.5 Business and Administrative Workflow Support (Part 2)
chunks.content:
might  be  better  as  predictable  rule-based  execution  can  be  simpler  to  validate 
and audit. Thus, agentic AI shouldn't be considered a “one-size-fits-all” solution to replace existing 
automation. What might be more suitable is a hybrid approach, where flexible AI parts interpret, and 
deterministic systems run tightly-specified operations.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.6 Software Development and Technical Assistance (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Another area where multi-step AI support could be beneficial is software development. Generative 
models could be used now to help explain, write and debug code; agentic workflows could be used 
to  coordinate  development  activities  more  broadly.  An  agentic  system  might  read  the  language  of 
the coding task and find the relevant project files and suggest changes, use the agreed development 
tools, check the test results and make further suggestions to its suggested implementation.  
The   opportunity   comes   from   generation   in   combination   with   feedback   from   the   outside.   An 
automated test provides a program that failed the test with information that can help in a next attempt. 
Yao et al. (2023) this is similar to the general trend of agenticness where observations made in the 
environment  are  used  as  inputs  for  subsequent  planning  or  actions.  Similarly,  tool-augmented 
architectures show that the capabilities of models can be expanded using tools as opposed to relying 
on their own answers (Mialon et al., 2023).  
However, there are reliabi

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.6 Software Development and Technical Assistance (Part 2)
chunks.content:
the capabilities of models can be expanded using tools as opposed to relying 
on their own answers (Mialon et al., 2023).  
However, there are reliability and security issues when it comes to automated code generation. Even 
if code is executed successfully, it doesn't necessarily mean the code itself is secure, maintainable 
or  requirements  compliant.  Hence,  when  agentic  techniques  are  applied  to  software  engineering, 
human  review,  automated  testing,  restricted  permissions  and  version-control  mechanisms  are 
important.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.7 Research and Knowledge-Management Support (Part 1)
chunks.content:
29 
It is often necessary to gather information, to organise it and to present it in a structured manner in 
the course of research and knowledge-management activities. Agentic workflows might be helpful 
with tasks like organising research notes, categorizing documents, creating structured reading lists, 
maintaining unresolved questions and coordinating retrieval from approved knowledge sources. This 
requires the difference between organisational support and academic judgement to be upheld and 
the usefulness of such systems relies on this.  
The mechanics of information management can be assisted by an agent, but the decisions as to the 
quality  of  the  sources,  methodological  validity,  interpretation,  and  academic  argumentation  are 
human.  This  is  especially  relevant  in  the  case  of  language,  where  a  fluently  produced  factually 
incorrect statement or an unsupported conclusion may be hard to identify. In tasks such as customer 
support that rely heavily on knowledge, the same scenarios exist, with an AI system being able to 
keep track of the context, acces

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.7 Research and Knowledge-Management Support (Part 2)
chunks.content:
such as customer 
support that rely heavily on knowledge, the same scenarios exist, with an AI system being able to 
keep track of the context, access relevant knowledge, and decide if escalation is necessary. Human 
centred design principles are still relevant as users require a way to 'take charge' if automation is not 
suitable, to 'correct' the system if it is wrong, and to understand its limitations (Amershi et al., 2019).

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.8 Conditions for Effective Adoption (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic AI has its practical value based on the context of its application. First, it is important that the 
goal is well defined, so that the system can find out what actions to take. Secondly, the agent should 
have control over the tools and data it is provided with and they should be relevant to the task. Third, 
at intermediate stages, intermediate outputs should be validated, where they may get amplified into 
later  stages.  Fourth,  where  it  involves  actions  to  external  systems  and/or  consequential  decision-
making, there must be meaningful human oversight to automation. Lastly, there should be reliability 
and constraint compliance taken into account as well as plausibility of output.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 5.9 Chapter Summary
chunks.content:
The opportunities Agentic AI provides for task automation were discussed in this chapter, responding 
to  RQ3.  The  literature  indicates  that  there  is  a  vast  potential  to  expand  AI  support  from  individual 
content creation to multi-step support. Agentic architectures may provide for more flexible tasks than 
traditional  deterministic  automation  and  one-shot  generative  interaction  through  a  combination  of 
goal interpretation, task decomposition, planning, maintained context, tool interaction, feedback and 
iterative correction.  
Applications  might  be  productivity  support,  personalised  organisation,  educational  study  planning, 
business  administration,  software  development,  research  support,  customer  service  and  personal 
task management. But the potential should not be read as proof of a benefit of Agentic AI in all areas.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 5. Opportunities of Agentic AI for Task Automation
chunks.content:
31 
Conventional RPA is still relevant for many processes that have a very stable and structured nature, 
while  the  relevance  of  agentic  systems  increases  when  processes  need  to  be  interpreted  and 
adapted.  
Therefore, the answer to RQ3 is that opportunities for Agentic AI can primarily be found in the flexible 
coordination  of  multi-step  task  automation,  where  goals  need  to  be  broken  down,  contextual 
information  needs  to  be  kept  track  of,  or  external  tools  or feedback  should  impact  subsequent 
actions.  This  is  provided  consistent  information,  secure  access  to  tools,  proper  validation,  well-
defined tasks, and meaningful supervision is provided. The risk with these requirements is looked at 
in Chapter 6.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 6.1 Hallucination and Factual Inaccuracy (Part 1)
chunks.content:
32 
One of the main challenges of language-model based systems is still hallucination. Ji et al. (2023) 
describe hallucination as generated content that is unsupported by, inconsistent with, or insufficiently 
grounded  in  the  available  source  information.  This  failure  can  lead  to  a  wrong  answer  in  normal 
conversational  system.  In  an  agentic  workflow,  however,  the  consequences  can  be  much  more 
profound, since the text generated by the model can be fed into other automated processes such as 
planning, tool selection or other automated processes.  
However, this is not to be confused with other agent failures that may occur. Even if the workflow 
around a model is correct, there is a possibility that a model gives an incorrect factual statement. In 
contrast,  if  the  system  chooses  the  wrong  action,  even  though  the  model  response  is  factually 
correct, the task will be considered failed. Hallucination is thus not the only aspect of the overall risk 
profile of Agentic AI.  
Bender et al. (2021) highlight that large language models are producing

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 6.1 Hallucination and Factual Inaccuracy (Part 2)
chunks.content:
tion is thus not the only aspect of the overall risk 
profile of Agentic AI.  
Bender et al. (2021) highlight that large language models are producing language based on learning 
statistical patterns in big data, and not validation of the truth of each statement. This is still the case 
when integrating an LLM into an agent. Output validation, based on trustworthy external information, 
and  explicit  review  mechanisms  can  decrease  risks  of  exposure  to  unsupported  content. These 
measures may reduce the risk of unsupported content, but they do not ensure factual correctness in 
all cases..

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 6.2 Planning and Reasoning Failures (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Agentic systems are characterized by an extra set of failure modes, as they not only have to decide 
what to generate, but also what to do next. Planning errors include breaking down a valid objective 
into  the  wrong  steps;  ignoring  constraints;  picking  wrong  order;  and/or  creating  tasks  that  are  not 
achievable with available tools. Wang et al. (2024) recognise planning as a key architectural aspect 
of  LLM-based  autonomous  agents  and  point  out  the  general  challenges  in  empowering  LLMs  to 
handle multi-step tasks.  
A conceptually different error from a planning error is a reasoning error. By reasoning we are referring 
here to the computational process to evaluate the information or to decide on an action; planning is 
related to the organisation of actions over multiple stages. For instance, a proposed workload can 
be  scheduled  at  a  deadline  that  the  agent  identified  correctly,  but  the  agent  could  be  wrong  in 
determining that the workload will be completed within the deadline. Or, the individual calculations 
might be valid, but the who

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 6.2 Planning and Reasoning Failures (Part 2)
chunks.content:
ould  be  wrong  in 
determining that the workload will be completed within the deadline. Or, the individual calculations 
might be valid, but the whole set of instructions still may not be feasible.  
These  differences  are  important  for  the  purposes  of  controls  because  different  errors  will  need 
different  controls.  Factual  validation  could  be  to  check  for  hallucination,  while  explicit  constraint 
checking  could  be  more  to  check  a  plan  that  is  infeasible. But  agentic  systems  take  advantage  of

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → Chapter 6. Challenges, Risks, and Responsible Use of Agentic AI
chunks.content:
33 
layered validation, instead of using a general-purpose model to check and approve each step in its 
process.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 6.3 Error Propagation Across Multi-Step Workflows (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Multi-step execution will allow the dependency structure: output of one step as input to the next step. 
Later components may act in line with the incorrect assumption if it is made in the early stage. This 
can   be   considered   to   be   an   error   propagation   process.   But   an   agentic   workflow   does   not 
automatically  mean  that  it  magnifies  errors.  The  error  propagation  can  be  dependent  on  the 
architecture, availability of independent checks, reversibility of actions and opportunities for human 
intervention.  
Several  sources  of  failure  can  be  distinguished  and  of  these  are  the  following  useful.  Model 
hallucination  is  a  problem  with  the  content  that  the  model  generates  but  that  the  model  doesn't

wrong tools, or wrong parameters. Data errors happen because data is incomplete, out-of-date, or

unreliable  agent.  Intermediate  validation  can  minimize  propagation  of  errors  as  output  from  one
