Reliability  is  the  ability  to  perform  the  intended  functions  without  interruption  when  conditions  are 
specified. In the case of Agentic AI, it's not just about the quality of the text itself, but also the reliability 
in planning and utilizing tools, adhering to constraints, and completing the task. The results of the 
language model can fluctuate from one run of the language model to another, and the results from 
external  services  can  also  change  without  regard  to  the  agent.  This  makes  it  harder  to  achieve 
reproducibility in an agentic workflow, than in a deterministic software procedure.  
Bommasani  et  al.  (2023)  propose  the  evaluation  of  language  models  be  done  along  multiple 
dimensions,  instead  of  a  single  performance  measure.  For  agents,  this  is  even  more  crucial:  A 
seemingly  successful  final  product  can  mask  problems  or  unsafe  operations in  between.  Hence, 
schema  validity,  completion  of  the  task,  constraint  compliance,  number  of  errors  or  warnings, 
correctness of the tools, the time of executio

correctness of the tools, the time of execution, human involvement required and/or the replicability 
of the results can all be taken into account for reliability assessment.

however,  has  design  considerations  as  traces  might  contain  sensitive  information.  So,  there  is  a

chunks.content:
Agentic AI can hold context, call external services, read structured files, and create execution logs, 
all of which can provide it with more information than a traditional, single-response application. Data 
minimisation becomes further important as a result of these capabilities. The information collected 
through the system should be retained and only access to sensitive information should be allowed 
based on the operational need.  
For  example  privacy  risks  can  be  encountered  when  storing  personal  information  in  persistent 
memory,  sharing  personal  information  with  third  party  model  providers,  storing  in  logs,  and 
unnecessarily sending personal information from agent to agent or tool. The data boundary of the 
system  is  also  altered  with  external  API  integration  since  data  might  exit  the  local  system.  Some 
appropriate  control  measures  are  limiting  the  amount  of  data  stored,  the  separation  of  credentials 
from   application   code,   restricting   access   rights,   removing   traces   of   unnecessary   personal 
information,

chunks.content:

from   application   code,   restricting   access   rights,   removing   traces   of   unnecessary   personal 
information, and establishment of retention periods.  
The  NIST  Artificial  Intelligence  Risk  Management  Framework  emphasises  the  importance  of 
governing  AI  risks  throughout  the  system  lifecycle  rather  than  viewing  risk  management  as  a  one 
time  technical  tick,  Tabassi  (2023).  The  Generative  AI  Profile  also  applies  risk-management 
principles to attributes of generative AI systems such as information integrity, privacy, security and 
human oversight (Autio et al., 2024). Although these publications are not based on empirical Agentic 
AI studies, but are standards oriented guidance, they offer a helpful framework for identifying controls 
that can be applied to agentic systems.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 6.6 Security Risks and Tool Misuse
chunks.content:
One of the main sources of capabilities and risks is the integration of tools. The consequence profile 
of  a  text  generation  model  that  cannot  take  external  actions  is  different  from  that  of  an  agent  that 
can   change   files,   call   APIs,   run   software   or   send   information   to   other   systems.   Excessive 
permissions can make an innocent model output into an action that has an external consequence.  
External  misleading  or  malicious  input,  prompt  injection,  unauthorized  use  of  authorized  tools, 
unintentional data exposure, or operation autonomy are potential security concerns. Prompt injection 
is especially relevant for an agent that processes content from outside that might contain instructions 
that conflict with the instructions of the original task. The danger isn't just that the model will generate 
the wrong kind of text: it could be that it chooses a different set of tools, or reveals different bits of 
information.

that  were  involved,  use  of  external  tools,  validation  success/fail  and  when  human  input  was

Execution  traces  can  be  used  to  increase  the  visibility  of  the  operations  while  preserving  the  key 
events  that  have  occurred  without  revealing  private  model  reasoning.  This  distinction  is  helpful 
because a system is accountable, but does not need to disclose all of its internal "chain of thought". 
System  auditing  is  supported  by  more  suitable  evidence  in  the  form  of  structured  records  of  task 
states, chosen tools, the outcome of validation and eventual decisions.

Evaluation  is  difficult  especially  since  the  quality  of  the  final  text  product  may  not  be  sufficient  to

"ramp up" on a task and therefore not have a simplistic completion metric but do the right thing risk 
management-wise. In contrast to evaluating static question answering, AgentBench shows the need 
to  evaluate  LLMs  as  interactive  agents  in  environments  (Liu  et  al.,  2024).  Thus,  the  evaluation  of 
agents can be based on a number of factors, such as task completion, respecting constraints, using 
the   tools   correctly,   presence   of   unsafe   actions,   number   of   errors   found,   amount   of   human 
intervention, and time or computational cost.  
Bommasani et al. (2023) also advocate for a multi-dimensional assessment of models, as opposed 
to collapsing it into one measure. This principle would seem to make it a good idea to use m

to collapsing it into one measure. This principle would seem to make it a good idea to use multiple

checking.  By  stopping  uncontrolled  outputs  to  automatically  be passed  to  subsequent  stages, 
intermediate  review  can  help  to  minimise  error  propagation.  Minimising  the  data  can  reduce  the 
impact  on  privacy.  Tool  allowlisting  helps  to  limit  what  actions  can  be  performed  by  the  system.

Design,   deployment,   operation   and   revision   of   Responsible   Agentic   AI   must   involve   risk 
management.  Tabassi  (2023)  defines  AI  risk  management  in  terms  of  governance,  mapping, 
measurement and management activities and, Autio et al. (2024) relocates the general framework 
to the specific risks around generative AI. These frameworks allow a lifecycle thinking where risks 
are to be identified before deployment and be monitored as the behaviour or operational context of 
the system evolve.  
With  agentic  systems,  the  concept  of  responsible  design  should  start  with  a  decision  whether  we 
actually need to have autonomous systems running or not. Tasks that have important consequences 
can be given lower levels of autonomy and/or can require human approval. Restrict use of tools to 
those necessary for the job; take actions that can be undone, if needed; systems should fail safely 
if information or resources are missing.  
The other aspect of governance in which clarity is required is on system limitation. It should not be 
assumed that an age

assumed that an agent is reliable and trustworthy because it can perform several steps on its own.

Responsible  governance  is  able  to  minimise  risks,  but  not  uncertainties.  A  probabilistic  model  in 
agentic  systems  is  a  mixture  of  probabilistic  model  elements,  software  components,  data  sources 
and human decisions, all of which may fail in isolation or in an unanticipated manner. Therefore it is 
necessary to have to not only a technical control, but organisational accountability also.

The preceding chapters examined the concepts, architectures, and potential applications of Agentic

The  analysis  shows  that  Agentic  AI  comes  with  a  number  of  interrelated  categories  of  risk.  Model

Agentic workflows have a number of stages that are dependent on each other so that the result of 
one  stage  can  impact on  the  results  of  the  others  (this  can  be  minimised  with  good  intermediate 
validation).  
The  more  data  is  kept  by  agents  or  the  more  they  communicate  with  other  tools,  the  greater  the 
potential   privacy   or   security   concerns.   Additionally,   transparency   or   accountability   is   more 
challengin

Rule mode is a way of planning deterministically and then reviewing explicitly with the rules, and if

external   LLM,   but   provides   local   valid

Study   planning   was   chosen   as   it   includes   several   operations   which   can   be   transparently

into account time available each day, scheduling work and checking deadlines.  
For instance, a user can define preparing for a Python exam as well as the topics, the dates and the 
number of hours available for study. These limitations become a organized plan by the system. This 
is  a  good  illustration  of  planning  and  task  decomposition  without  the  additional  dangers  of  "freely 
allowed outside actions".  
But  it  is  not  an  educational  context  which  indicates  that  the  system  enhances  the  learning 
performance.  The  prototype  measures  functional  planning  behaviour,  not  the  achievement  of  the

The prototype is executed by four main ideas of design.  
Modularity is the first step, which is to separate input validation, planning, data access, data review, 
revision, orchestration and output handling. This facilitates audit of the different steps of the workflow.  
Secondly the system is of bounded autonomy. Revision is only allowed two times, there are limited 
tools  and  approval  is  given  prior  to  the  final  product  being  accepted.  This  is  in  line  with  human-
centred  methods  that  integrate  the  capabilities  of  automated systems  with  the  sense  of  human 
agency in the system (Amershi et al., 2019; Shneiderman, 2020).  
Thirdly, access to these tools is purposefully limited. The application is designed to read allowlisted 
local data files (JSON, CSV) and does not provide access to the file system, shell, the internet or a 
database. Fourth, there is accent on traceability in the system.  
The  execution  trace  is  used  to  record  important  operations  rather  than  using  internal  model 
reasoning which is inaccessible.

chunks.content:
Three software validation methods that were complementary were used.  
Pytest is a system that tests behaviour of automated test suite. The last run reported by the authors

Ruff is a configured, static-source-code-analysis tool.  
The result reported was:  
All checks passed. Mypy is a static typechecker.  
The outcome reported was: No problems were detected in 17 source files: Success.

These results provide technical software-quality evidence under the tested conditions. Ruff and Mypy 
do not assess the educational quality of generated study plans, while passing automated tests does 
not establish reliability beyond the behaviours covered by the test suite.  
The  tests  also  verify  that  the  revision  limit  is  set  to  two  tries,  and  that  the  revision  system  can  fail

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 7.13 Relationship Between the Prototype and Agentic AI Theory
chunks.content:
45 
The prototype relies on Agentic AI mainly at the workflow-level and not as a case of free reign of the 
model. Validated input is goal interpretation, planner is planning, controlled access to JSON/CSVs 
are tools, execution-scoped memory is state, reviewers' output is feedback, bounded correction is 
revision, approval is oversight and execution tracing is accountability.  
The design thus represents the general architectural perspective of the previous chapters, in which 
an agentic system is not just an LLM, but a coordinated workflow that includes mechanisms to plan, 
interact with, collect feedback from, and execute the LLM in a controlled fashion.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 7.14 Prototype Limitations
chunks.content:
This is a prototype still with some restrictions. Study data and effort estimates are fictional, the task 
domain is small and the evaluation includes a small authored case set. The quality of the reviews is 
based   on   manual   rules.   No   human-participant   study or   some   form   of   educational-outcome 
assessment was performed.  
LLM-assisted  mode  requires  an  external  service  to  be  enabled  and  will  revert  to  deterministic 
planning  in  the  event  that  the  API,  SDK,  key  or  planned-for  response  schema  is  unavailable. 
Production deployment and comprehensive penetration testing of the application was not performed. 
Therefore, the results of the study cannot be generalized beyond the functional assessment used.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 7.15 Chapter Summary
chunks.content:
This  chapter  addressed  RQ5:  How  can  a  lightweight  prototype  demonstrate  the  basic  workflow  of 
an Agentic AI system? 
The prototype that we have implemented implements such a workflow, which includes validated goal 
input,   task   planning,   restricted   structured-data   tools,   execution-scoped   state,   explicit   review, 
bounded revision, approval, structured outputs and factual execution tracing. Automated tests further 
verify  that  revision  is  bounded  and  that  selected  intentionally  introduced  defects  can  be  corrected 
under the tested conditions.  
Different  results  were  obtained  in  the  functional  evaluation  when  the  agent  was  operating  in  one-
shot  baseline  and  rule-based  modes,  such  as  the  number  of  times  the  reviewer  passed  (71.4% 
versus 100.0%) and the mean number of validation error counts (0.571 versus 0.000). These findings 
are on a small scale and are functional. They don't show enhanced education results, unrestricted 
reliability, readiness to produce or overall superiority over other Agentic AI systems.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.1 Summary of the Study
chunks.content:
46 
This thesis focused on Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AAI) by conducting a structured literature-based 
analysis and generating a simple Python prototype as a new method for task automation. The study 
began  by  differentiating  Agentic  AI  from  traditional  chatbots,  robotic  process  automation,  and 
generative  AI  assistants  and  from  conventional  AI  systems.  It  then  examined  the  key  elements  of 
agentic workflows, how they might be used, and the technical and governance issues that arise as 
agentic workflows become more automated. The theoretical analysis was supported by an Agentic 
Study-Planning  System  which  turned  the  selected  concepts  into  a  software  workflow  that  is 
transparent and bounded.  
The findings in the study suggest that the most suitable level to approach Agentic AI is the system 
level.  Its  value  isn't  in  using  an  LLM  only,  it's  in  orchestrating  models,  planning  processes,  state, 
tools, feedback, validation and human oversight to a clear goal.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.2 Answer to Research Question 1
chunks.content:
RQ1  addressed  the  question  of  how  Agentic  AI  differs  from  the  traditional  chatbots  and  general 
generative AI systems. The analysis reveals that being goal-directed and operating in a multi-step 
manner are the primary features of Agentic AI. Traditional chatbots are more reactive, and generative 
AI  assistants  are  more  likely  to  focus  on  generating  outputs  based  on  instructions.  These  can  be 
extended  by  agentic  architectures,  which  can  plan,  maintain  state  or  memory,  interact  with  tools, 
feedback and control their execution.  
Agentic  AI  is  not,  however,  universally  and  standardised  defined.  As  generative  assistants  evolve 
into more agentic systems, the lines start to blur between the two, as traditional assistants now have 
a memory, incorporate planning and tools, and orchestrate workflows.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.3 Answer to Research Question 2
chunks.content:
RQ2 investigated the main components and work processes of Agentic AI systems. The literature 
revealed  the  following  functions  frequently  recurring:  Goal  interpretation,  task  decomposition, 
planning,  maintaining  the  state  or  memory,  interaction  with  tools, action  generation,  feedback, 
revision, monitoring execution and human supervision. These components are not required universal 
components. Whether they are implemented is dependent on the level of complexity of the task, the 
tools  available,  the  level  of reliability  required,  and  the  level  of  autonomy  thought  fit.  Thus,  single-
agent and multi-agent designs are not sequentially better Agentic AI types, but instead are design 
patterns.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.4 Answer to Research Question 3
chunks.content:
47 
The opportunities for task automation using Agentic AI was discussed in RQ3. The main advantage 
is to have the freedom to plan activities that take place in multiple steps and aren't hardwired or just 
a  single  text.  It  could  be  used  for  productivity  support,  study  planning,  administration  processes, 
software-development support, research-organisation and so on.  
These  opportunities  are  not  guaranteed  but  are  conditional.  In  regards  to  the  latter,  agentic 
automation  can  be  useful  when  interpretation,  planning,  context  maintenance  and  adaptation  are 
needed,  whereas  deterministic  automation  might  be  appropriate  for  stable  and  very  predictable 
processes.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.5 Answer to Research Question 4
chunks.content:
RQ4 focused on the challenges that impact the use of Agentic AI in a safe and reliable way. There 
are  significant  limitations,  such  as  hallucination,  planning  and  reasoning  errors,  propagation  of 
errors, privacy exposure, security risks, inappropriate use of the tools, difficulties in evaluation, and 
ambiguity in accountability.  
Reliability needs to be thought about on a system level as failures may occur due to Models, Data, 
Tools, Orchestration or external systems. While risks can be lowered through validation, constrained 
permissions,  tool  allowlisting,  bounded  revision,  execution  traces,  graceful  failure  and  human 
approval, risks cannot be eliminated.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.6 Answer to Research Question 5
chunks.content:
RQ5: How can a lightweight prototype show a simple Agentic AI process? This was achieved in the 
prototype developed in the study planning through the input and validation of goals, planning with 
structure,  interaction  with  JSON  and  CSV  data,  maintaining  session  state,  reviewing  the  plan, 
bounded revision capability, human approval, generation of structured output and execution tracing.  
Technical  validation  included  30  passing  automated  tests,  successful  Ruff  analysis,  and  Mypy 
analysis reporting no issues in 17 source files. These results demonstrate technical validation within 
the  tested  conditions,  not  educational  effectiveness,  production  readiness,  or  general  Agentic  AI 
performance.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.7 Theoretical and Practical Contributions
chunks.content:
This thesis' chief advantage is the inclusion of an orderly synthesis of Agentic AI at the bachelor level 
as  well  as  a  clear  and  understandable  practical  demonstration.  The  theoretical  part  explains  the 
difference  between  agentic  systems  and  traditional  generative  interfaces  as  well  as  the  common 
elements, opportunities and dangers of agentic systems. The practical part shows how these ideas 
can be applied to a limited Python workflow without giving free rein to the autonomy.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.8 Recommendations for Responsible Implementation
chunks.content:
48 
Agentic systems should be designed by taking into account the consequences of their actions. Only 
give the tools to people what they need to do, intermediate results must be verified, consequential 
actions  must  be  under  the  control  of  humans,  and  execution traces  must  be  established  for 
accountabilities  to  be  met.  Increasing  autonomy  should  thus  only  be  done  if  this  has  an  obvious 
functional benefit and if suitable protection measures exist.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.9 Limitations of the Thesis
chunks.content:
The  thesis  has  limitation  because  of  the  limited  scope  of  prototype  and  the  limited  functional 
evaluation. Implementation involves the use of local or fictional study data, is mostly rule-based, and 
does  not  involve  human-participant  study.  No  education  outcomes  were  measured  and  thus  the 
results do not show an impact on education. The optional LLM-assisted mode requires that one has 
to  use  an  external  model  when  it  is  turned  on,  and  the  narrow  task  domain  does  not  allow  for 
generalisability to other applications.

chunks.heading: Zubair_Ahmed_Khan_92127983_Bachelor_Thesis.pdf → 8.10 Directions for Future Research (Part 1)
chunks.content:
Some future studies would be to validate the architecture with a larger and more varied task sets, 
controlled studies with users, and comparisons with other agent designs. Future studies can be done 
to improve the validation mechanisms, add other controlled tools, perform specific security tests and 
offer  a  comparison  of  the  planning  process  using  a  rule-based  system  and  the  LLM.  Longitudinal 
educational studies would also have to be carried out to be able to measure if there is any effect of 
agent-supported study planning on learner outcomes.  
There are other areas that could be systematically evaluated, such as cost, latency, reliability and 
human-intervention requirements. To sum up: Agentic AI can be a valuable architectural solution for 
orchestrating  goal-driven  task  automation;  however,  it needs  bounded  autonomy,  transparent 
system  behaviors,  strong  validation  mechanisms,  limited  access  to  tools  and  resources,  and 
meaningful human oversight.

1. Introduction and Problem Statement
Artificial intelligence has developed rapidly from rule-based systems and traditional machine learning models to 
modern generative AI systems that can understand prompts, generate text, summarize information, assist with 
coding,  and  support  decision-making  tasks. A  recent  and  important  development  in  this  field  is Agentic AI. 
Unlike  ordinary  chatbots  that  mainly  respond  to  a  single  prompt,  agentic AI  systems  are  designed  to  work 
toward  a  goal  by  planning  steps,  using  tools,  processing  information,  and  adjusting  their  output  based  on

automation. For example, an agentic AI system can help create a study plan, summarize documents, organize 
research notes, generate a to-do list, or support simple workflow automation. These systems are usually built 
around large language models and may include components such as planning, memory, tool use, and human 
supervision. Because of this, agentic AI has the potential to improve productivity and reduce repetitive work.
However, agentic AI also introduces important challenges. Since such systems can perform multi-step tasks, 
an  incorrect  decision  at  one  stage  may  affect  the  final  output.  Common  problems  include  hallucination, 
unreliable  reasoning,  weak  evaluation  methods,  privacy  concerns,  tool  misuse,  and  lack  of  accountability.

The current literature discusses autonomous agents, large language model-based agents, tool use, multi-agent

The  aim  of  this  bachelor  thesis  is  to  analyze  agentic  AI  for  task  automation  from  a  mainly  theoretical

The thesis provides students with the opportunity “to demonstrate some originality in identifying a topic or a line of 
argument and to follow up their insight with a more systematic piece of research work” (Dunleavy, 1986, p. 110). This 
Thesis Handbook represents a detailed guide to writing your thesis at IU. 
A  thesis  is  an  academic  research  paper  which  incorporates  theory  and  application  in  equal  measure.  It  includes  the 
academic research of a topic that is relevant to a corresponding academic field.  The thesis should demonstrate that  you

A thesis can only be completed successfully if: (1) you are really interested in the topic, (2) you are willing to become an

chunks.heading: README.md → Agentic Study Task Planning System
chunks.content:
A reproducible command-line research prototype supporting the bachelor thesis
“A Literature-Based Analysis of Agentic AI for Task Automation: Opportunities,
Challenges, and a Lightweight Prototype Demonstration.”

This is a bounded demonstration, not a production application, educational adviser,
benchmark, or general-purpose autonomous agent. Course data and effort estimates are
fictional. A person remains responsible for accepting, changing, or rejecting every plan.

chunks.heading: README.md → Features
chunks.content:
- Deterministic rule mode that needs no API key or internet connection
- One-shot baseline for an illustrative functional comparison
- Optional OpenAI-assisted draft generation with structured JSON, local validation, and
  deterministic fallback
- Allowlisted JSON/CSV data tools with project-directory path restrictions
- Capacity-aware task breakdown, priorities, durations, dates, recap, and exam assessment
- Explicit rule-based critique and a maximum of two correction attempts
- Execution-scoped memory, factual JSON trace, structured plan, and readable Markdown
- Interactive approval plus clearly labelled auto-approval for automated demonstrations

chunks.heading: README.md → Architecture
chunks.content:
The CLI validates a goal, the agent loads local course and availability data, and the
planner creates a draft. In agent modes a reviewer evaluates explicit rules and sends
structured issue codes to deterministic revision rules, at most twice. Approval precedes
final output. Baseline mode deliberately omits critique and revision but uses the same
validated input. See [architecture](docs/architecture.md) and
[implementation details](docs/implementation.md).

chunks.heading: README.md → Requirements and installation
chunks.content:
- Python 3.11 or newer
- No runtime dependency for deterministic operation
- Matplotlib for figures; OpenAI SDK only for optional LLM mode

```bash
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate              # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Optional LLM support:

```bash
python -m pip install -e ".[llm]"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="..."            # never put the value in this repository
export OPENAI_MODEL="gpt-5.6-sol"       # optional override
study-planner --demo --mode llm --auto-approve
```

If the key, SDK, API, or returned schema is unavailable/invalid, LLM mode records the
provider/model metadata and safely uses the deterministic planner. No secret is logged.

chunks.heading: README.md → Usage
chunks.content:
```bash
study-planner --help
study-planner --demo --mode rule --auto-approve
study-planner --goal-file data/sample_goals.json --goal-index 0 --mode rule --auto-approve
python -m study_planner --demo --mode rule --auto-approve
python scripts/run_demo.py
python scripts/run_evaluation.py
python scripts/generate_figures.py
```

Without `--demo` or `--goal-file`, the CLI requests a goal, subjects, and dates, then
offers approve, regenerate, or cancel. `--auto-approve` is only an automation mechanism;
its stored status does not claim external human review.

chunks.heading: README.md → Quality checks
chunks.content:
```bash
python -m pytest -q
python -m ruff check .
python -m mypy src
```

Each successful run writes `plan.json`, `study_plan.md`, `execution_trace.json`, and
`review_metadata.json` under `results/demonstrations/<run-id>/`. Evaluation CSV, JSON,
and report files go to `results/evaluation/`; figures go to `results/figures/`.

chunks.heading: README.md → Privacy, security, and limitations
chunks.content:
The application has no arbitrary shell, internet, database, persistent personal memory,
authentication, or unrestricted file tool. Data reads are restricted to `data/`, writes
to `results/`, and traces contain factual summaries rather than private reasoning.
Interactive goal content is stored in output by design, so users should avoid sensitive
information. Rule quality depends on authored heuristics and fictional effort estimates.
The small evaluation cannot establish effectiveness beyond its cases. LLM behavior can
vary and always remains subject to local validation and human approval.

chunks.heading: README.md → Troubleshooting
chunks.content:
- “requires Python >=3.11”: invoke a newer interpreter explicitly.
- Goal rejected: use ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`, a deadline on/after start, and positive capacity.
- Figure import error: install `.[figures]` or `.[dev]`.
- LLM fallback: verify `OPENAI_API_KEY`, optional SDK installation, model access, and
  network availability. Rule mode remains fully usable.

chunks.heading: README.md → Repository structure
chunks.content:
```text
data/                   fictional courses, availability, goals, evaluation cases
src/study_planner/      typed workflow modules and CLI
scripts/                demonstrations, evaluation, figures
tests/                  deterministic pytest suite
docs/                   architecture, method, mapping, reproducibility, rubric
results/                generated evidence
```
